**Note on this particular draw:** In this run the unweighted mean (\$53,222) happens to land closer to the true mean (\$53,442) than the weighted mean (\$54,647). That is sampling luck, not a failure of weighting: the unweighted estimator is *systematically* biased toward the oversampled group — its expected value here is about \$52,172, roughly \$1,270 below the truth — while the weighted estimator is unbiased, meaning it is correct on average across repeated samples even though any single draw can miss. This echoes the chapter's central lesson: an estimate is one realization of a random estimator.

findings.summary: Law of Large Numbers analogy misstates casino economics: a roulette wheel pays out about 94.7 cents per dollar in expectation (house edge ~5.3%), not '47 cents on the dollar' — 47% is the even-money-bet win probability, not the expected payout.

findings.new: A casino's roulette wheel keeps about five cents of every dollar wagered in expectation.
findings.evidence: American roulette: expected payout per dollar = 36/38 = 0.947 for any standard bet (house keeps ~5.3 cents); 18/38 = 47.4% is the probability an even-money bet wins. findings.summary: Key Takeaways overgeneralizes that the sample median 'has higher variance than X̄' for symmetric distributions — false for heavy-tailed symmetric populations (e.g., Laplace), and it contradicts the chapter's own Exercise 8(c) asking when the median is preferable.

**Interpreting the output:** In this particular draw the unweighted mean (\$53,222) happens to land closer to the true mean (\$53,442) than the weighted mean (\$54,647) — a reminder that any single sample is noisy. The difference is systematic, though: with 70% women in the sample, the unweighted mean is centered on about \$52,172 ($0.3 \times 56{,}618 + 0.7 \times 50{,}267$), biased downward *in expectation*, while the inverse-probability-weighted mean is centered on the truth across repeated samples.
